opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few really important differences, and some of them cut in opposite directions.

The first is just the ratio. In a traditional company, a manager might oversee maybe five to ten direct reports, and there's a natural limit because you need time to understand what each person is doing, build trust, give feedback. With AI agents, you could easily imagine one person nominally "supervising" hundreds or thousands of agents running in parallel. And so the question becomes: what does supervision even mean at that scale? You can't read everything they produce. You can't sit in on every decision. So a lot of the oversight has to be delegated, and the natural thing to delegate it to is other AI systems. That's where you get into things like scalable oversight, where you're using AI to help humans evaluate AI, and the hierarchy starts to look less like a pyramid of people and more like a pyramid where most of the layers are models checking other models, with humans at key points.

The second difference is about trust and incentives. In a company, you rely on a lot of implicit mechanisms: people have reputations, careers, legal liability, social norms, they care what their colleagues think. Those are actually doing a huge amount of work in keeping organizations functioning, and we mostly don't notice it. AI agents don't have most of that. They don't have a career they're worried about. So you can't lean on those mechanisms, and you have to replace them with something more explicit: monitoring, interpretability, evaluations, careful permissions. On the flip side, you have affordances you never have with humans. You can rerun the same situation many times, look at counterfactuals, inspect internal activations in principle, red-team an agent before deploying it. You can't do that with an employee.

Third, there's the question of correlated failure. In a human organization, people are diverse. If one person has a bad idea or bad values, others will often push back. If you have a thousand copies of the same model, they might all share the same blind spot or the same subtle misalignment. So your "checks and balances" might be much weaker than they look on paper if the checker and the checked are basically the same mind. That's something I think people underappreciate. You probably want deliberate diversity, different models, different training, different prompts, so that the oversight layers are actually somewhat independent.

And then the last thing, which I think is the core alignment question: in a company, the employees are roughly as capable as the manager, sometimes more, but not wildly more. As AI systems get more capable, you could end up in a situation where the humans at the top genuinely can't evaluate whether the work is good. At that point the hierarchy only works if the systems are actually aligned, actually trying to do what we want, not just appearing to. Supervision buys you a lot in the near term, but I don't think it's a substitute for getting the alignment right. It's more like a way to bootstrap: use systems we can still verify to help us align and check the next generation, and try to keep that chain intact as capabilities go up.

So in short: much wider spans of control, much less reliance on implicit social trust, much more reliance on explicit technical oversight, and a real need to worry about everyone in the org making the same mistake at once.

r001.rationale: The response discusses oversight and task evaluation, but does not recommend assigning tasks according to whether AI systems or humans perform them better.

r002.rationale: It explains that traditional organizations rely on human-specific limits and mechanisms—such as manageable spans of control, reputation, careers, and social norms—that AI-agent organizations cannot rely on in the same way.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the obvious analogy is a company, right? You have a CEO, you have VPs, you have managers, and then individual contributors at the bottom, and information flows up and decisions flow down. And I think a lot of people, when they picture lots of AI agents working together, they just sort of transplant that org chart and replace the humans with models. And I think that's probably wrong, or at least it misses what's actually interesting.

The first thing that's different is that in a company, the hierarchy exists largely because of human limitations. A manager can only have maybe five to ten direct reports because they only have so much attention, so many hours in the day. Communication is lossy. People forget things. People have their own incentives, they want to get promoted, they don't want to look bad in front of their boss. A huge amount of corporate structure is basically a workaround for those constraints. And AI agents don't have most of those constraints, or they have very different ones. An agent can in principle supervise thousands of other agents. You can copy an agent. You can have it look at the full transcript of what another agent did rather than a summary that's been filtered through three layers of people who each had reasons to make it sound better than it was.

So I think the structures you'd want end up looking quite different. Something I think about a lot is that the hard part isn't really the agents coordinating with each other. The hard part is the interface between the humans and the system as a whole. Because if you have a million agents doing stuff, and you have, say, a few dozen humans who are nominally in charge, then the bottleneck is entirely on the human side. The humans cannot read everything. They cannot check everything. And so the question becomes: what do you show the humans, who decides what to show them, and how do you make sure that process itself is trustworthy?

In a traditional company you solve this partly through trust that's built up over time. You've worked with someone for ten years, you know they're competent, you know they won't lie to you, so you delegate. With AI systems, we don't yet have good ways to establish that kind of trust. We can't just interview the model and get a sense of its character, or at least we can't do that reliably. So I think a lot of the "management structure" for AI agents is actually going to be an oversight structure. You want agents whose job it is to monitor other agents, you want to be able to run the same task multiple times with different models and compare, you want to have the ability to audit any decision and trace it back. These are things a company does a little bit, with internal audit or compliance, but they're sort of peripheral. For AI systems I think they need to be central.

The other thing I'd say is that in a company, if your manager tells you to do something unethical or illegal, there's some chance you push back, you go to HR, you quit, you talk to a journalist. There are lots of independent humans with their own values embedded throughout the hierarchy, and that acts as a check. If all the layers are AI systems, you really want to make sure that property is preserved somehow, that the system doesn't just become a very efficient pipeline for executing whatever's at the top, including mistakes or misuse. And that's actually a pretty tricky design problem, because you also don't want agents that just refuse to do things all the time.

So I guess the short version is: the goal of a company hierarchy is to get a lot of work done despite humans being limited. The goal of a human-supervised AI system has to be to get a lot of work done while making sure the humans actually stay in control, and those two goals push you toward pretty different architectures.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI agents’ organizational roles and oversight, but does not recommend assigning them tasks based on whether they perform better or worse than humans.

r002.rationale: It explains that traditional hierarchies are largely workarounds for human limits such as finite attention, lossy communication, and incentives, so AI-agent structures would differ.

astra-6.text:
I think a company is a useful analogy, but there are some important differences. In a company, you delegate partly because you don’t have the time or expertise to do everything yourself. And you face a similar problem with AI agents: if you had to check every action in detail, you wouldn’t get much benefit from delegating.

But with AI, you might have a very large number of agents operating much faster than you can follow. So human supervision can’t just mean a person approving every step. You need some way of deciding which decisions require human attention, and how to give the human enough context to actually evaluate them.

You could have other AI systems helping with that oversight—checking work, identifying problems, explaining what happened. But then you have to ask: how do we know those systems are doing a good job? If the agent doing the work and the agent checking it have the same blind spots, adding another layer of management might not help very much.

So I’d expect the hierarchy to be more fluid than a traditional company’s. You can copy agents, run different approaches in parallel, and allocate more effort to checking a particularly consequential decision. The hard part is making sure that all of this preserves meaningful human control. Can the human understand the important choices, redirect what’s happening, and notice when the system is pursuing something they didn’t intend?

r001.rationale: The response discusses delegation limits and oversight, but does not recommend assigning tasks based on whether AI systems perform them better or worse than humans.

r002.rationale: It describes ways AI-agent hierarchies may differ, but does not attribute those differences to human organizations being designed around how people work together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy to a company is useful, but there are some pretty important differences. In a company, you have managers supervising other managers, and ultimately you’re relying on people’s judgment at every level. With AI agents, you might have a relatively small number of humans supervising a very large number of systems, many of which can do tasks that the humans can’t easily evaluate directly.

So the central question becomes: how do you make that supervision effective? If an agent produces a complicated piece of research, you don’t want the human’s job to just be reading it and saying, “Well, that looks convincing.” You want tools for checking the work, surfacing uncertainty, and identifying the parts where human judgment is actually needed. You can use other AI systems to help with that, but then you have to ask whether those systems are reliably catching mistakes or sharing the same blind spots.

Another difference is that you can copy an agent. You can run the same system on lots of tasks in parallel. That’s very useful, but it also means that having lots of agents doesn’t necessarily give you independent judgment in the way that having lots of different people might.

Ultimately, I’d want the structure to amplify human oversight: make it easier for people to understand what’s happening and intervene, even as they delegate more of the work. Simply putting a human at the top of an org chart doesn’t establish that they have meaningful control.

r001.rationale: The response discusses effective oversight and delegation but does not recommend preferentially assigning AI tasks it does better than humans.

r002.rationale: It contrasts human managers with AI agents, but does not attribute organizational differences to human organizations being tailored to how people work together.
